# Meningitis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Infections of the central nervous system > Meningitis*

[Original Article Link](/library/ZR0Zlf)

---

## Summary

Meningitis is an infection of the <u>meninges</u> in the <u>brain</u> or spinal cord. Common causes include <u>viruses</u> and bacteria, although fungal, parasitic, and noninfectious causes of meningitis are possible. The most common bacterial pathogens (<u>N. meningitidis</u>, <u>S. pneumoniae</u>, <u>H. influenzae</u>, Group B <u>streptococcus</u>, and <u>L. monocytogenes</u>) vary depending on age and underlying medical conditions. <u>Enteroviruses</u> and <u>herpes simplex virus</u> (<u>HSV</u>) are the leading causes of viral meningitis. The <u>classic triad of meningitis</u> (<u>fever</u>, <u>meningismus</u>, <u>altered mental state</u>) occurs in less than half of adult patients and <u>meningitis in children</u> frequently presents with nonspecific symptoms. Advanced infection includes <u>signs of increased intracranial pressure</u> (<u>ICP</u>), neurological deficits, <u>altered mental status</u>, and <u>seizures</u>. Diagnosis is confirmed with <u>CSF analysis</u> and microbiological studies (e.g., <u>PCR</u>, culture). If <u>increased ICP</u> is suspected, a CT of the head is recommended prior to <u>lumbar puncture</u> (<u>LP</u>). <u>Antibiotic therapy</u> should not be delayed for diagnostic testing. Bacterial meningitis requires rapid initiation of empiric antimicrobials and sometimes <u>glucocorticoids</u> to prevent complications, which include neurological deficits (e.g., <u>hearing loss</u>) and <u>end-organ damage</u> (e.g., <u>Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome</u> in patients with <u>meningococcal meningitis</u>). While most cases of viral meningitis are <u>self-limiting</u>, <u>herpesvirus</u> infections (e.g., <u>HSV</u>, <u>VZV</u>) must be promptly recognized and treated with IV <u>acyclovir</u> to prevent serious complications and <u>death</u>. Prevention is through <u>vaccination</u> against common causes of meningitis, and <u>chemoprophylaxis</u> for exposed contacts.




<u>Neonatal bacterial meningitis</u> is detailed separately.

---

## Etiology

### Common causes




* <u>Otitis media</u>

* <u>Sinusitis</u>

* <u>CSF leak</u> after <u>head trauma</u> or neurosurgery

* Maternal <u>group B streptococcal</u> infection during <u>birth</u>

* <u>Sepsis</u>





### <u>Risk factors</u>




* <u>Immunocompromise</u> (e.g., due to <u>AIDS</u>, <u>asplenia</u>, <u>heavy alcohol use</u> disorder, chronic illness, cancer, <u>sickle cell anemia</u>, old age, <u>pregnancy</u>)

* Crowded occupational or living conditions (e.g., college dormitories, military barracks, retirement homes, kindergartens)

* Close contact with an infected person

### Less common bacterial pathogens




* <u>Borrelia</u> spp. (<u>Lyme meningitis</u>)

* <u>Treponema pallidum</u> (<u>syphilitic meningitis</u>)

* <u>Mycobacterium tuberculosis</u> (<u>tuberculous meningitis</u>)

* <u>Actinomyces israelii</u>

* <u>Leptospira</u> (<u>leptospirosis</u>)





### Other etiologies




* Viral meningitis: often associated with <u>encephalitis</u> (<u>meningoencephalitis</u>)

* <u>Enteroviruses</u> (especially <u>coxsackieviruses</u> and <u>echoviruses</u>): the most common cause of all types of meningitis in all patient groups [[16]](/library/7mb4S8)

* <u>Herpesviruses</u>: <u>HSV</u> (meningitis is more commonly caused by <u>HSV2</u> than <u>HSV1</u>) , <u>CMV</u>, <u>EBV</u>, <u>VZV</u>

* <u>Lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus</u> (LCMV)

* <u>Mumps virus</u>

* <u>Measles virus</u>

* Some <u>arboviruses</u> (e.g., <u>West Nile virus</u>, <u>TBEV</u> in Eurasia)

* <u>Poliovirus</u> (nonparalytic <u>poliomyelitis</u>: aseptic meningitic form)

* <u>St. Louis encephalitis virus</u>

* <u>California encephalitis virus</u>

* <u>Western equine encephalitis</u> <u>virus</u>

* <u>Influenza virus</u>

* <u>HIV</u>

* <u>JC virus</u> [[17]](/library/n5b7k8)

* Fungal meningitis

* <u>Coccidioides</u>

* <u>Candida</u> spp.

* <u>Aspergillus</u> spp.

* Parasitic meningitis

* <u>Helminths</u> (e.g., <u>Echinococcus</u> spp., <u>Strongyloides stercoralis</u>, Angiostrongyliasis cantonensis, <u>Baylisascaris procyonis</u>)

* <u>Protozoa</u> (e.g., <u>Naegleria fowleri</u>; , <u>Acanthamoeba</u>)

* <u>Noninfectious meningitis</u>

* <u>Sarcoidosis</u>

* <u>Tumor</u> <u>metastases</u> (<u>meningeal carcinomatosis</u> and <u>meningeal leukemia</u>)

* Medication (e.g., <u>NSAIDs</u>, <u>sulfa drugs</u>) [[18]](/library/h5bcP8)





### Causes of meningitis in <u>immunocompromised individuals</u>




* Bacterial

* Certain <u>immune deficiencies</u> can predispose to certain types of meningitis. [[19]](/library/55bik8)

* Defects in <u>humoral immunity</u> (including <u>splenectomy</u>): <u>encapsulated bacteria</u> (<u>N. meningitidis</u>, <u>S. pneumoniae</u>, <u>H. influenzae</u>, etc.)

* Defects in cell-mediated <u>immunity</u> (e.g., in <u>HIV</u>, drug-induced <u>immunosuppression</u>): <u>M. tuberculosis</u>, <u>L. monocytogenes</u>

* <u>Immunocompromised individuals</u> are at increased risk of recurrent bacterial meningitis compared to those with intact <u>immunity</u>. [[14]](/library/O5bI48)

* Viral: Risk is higher in individuals with cell-mediated <u>immune deficiencies</u> (e.g., in <u>HIV infection</u>). [[20]](/library/65bjO8)

* <u>Herpesviruses</u>: <u>CMV</u>, <u>EBV</u>, <u>VZV</u>, and HSV6

* <u>HIV</u>

* <u>Adenovirus</u>

* <u>JC virus</u>  [[17]](/library/n5b7k8)

* Fungal: Risk is higher in individuals with cell-mediated <u>immune deficiencies</u> (e.g., <u>HIV infection</u>). [[21]](/library/I5bYl8)

* <u>Cryptococcus</u> spp.

* <u>Candida</u> spp.

* <u>Histoplasma capsulatum</u>

* <u>Aspergillus</u> spp.

* <u>Protozoal</u>: <u>Toxoplasma gondii</u> (rare) [[22]](/library/J5bsO8)

---

## Pathophysiology

### Pathways of infection




* Most pathogens that cause meningitis colonize the <u>nasopharynx</u> or the upper <u>airways</u> before entering the <u>CNS</u> via:

* Hematogenous dissemination  [[23]](/library/QKYuTJ)

* Contiguous spread of infections in nose, eyes, and <u>ears</u>

* Retrograde transport along or within peripheral or <u>cranial nerves</u>

* Direct infection (e.g., due to trauma or head <u>surgery</u>) [[24]](/library/iKYJTJ)





### Incubation periods




* Bacterial meningitis: usually 3–7 days [[25]](/library/yaadMQ)

* Viral meningitis: usually 2–14 days, depending on the type of <u>virus</u>





References:[[25]](/library/yaadMQ)[[26]](/library/U3ab34)

---

## Clinical features

Clinical features of bacterial and viral meningitis are similar, although viral meningitis is less acute and usually <u>self-limiting</u> within 5–14 days. [[27]](/library/L7Wwm50)




### <u>Symptoms of meningitis</u> [[4]](/library/_EY5yI)[[6]](/library/Od1IJf0)




* Classic triad of meningitis ;  [[6]](/library/Od1IJf0)[[28]](/library/1db2Ks)[[29]](/library/WdbPKs)

* <u>Fever</u>

* Meningismus

* <u>Headache</u>

* Neck stiffness

* <u>Photophobia</u>

* <u>Altered mental state</u>

* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>

* <u>Malaise</u>

* <u>Seizures</u>

* <u>Neonates</u> and young children often present with nonspecific symptoms (see also “<u>Meningitis in children</u>” and “<u>Neonatal bacterial meningitis</u>”)





#### <u>Pathogen</u>-specific symptoms




* Patients with <u>N. meningitidis</u>: signs of <u>meningococcemia</u>

* <u>Myalgia</u>: more common in children

* Possibly <u>petechial</u> or <u>purpuric</u> <u>rash</u>: more common in children

* Possibly <u>Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome</u>: more common in children [[30]](/library/JjdsYJ0)

* Patients with viral meningitis

* <u>Prodrome</u> with <u>flu-like symptoms</u>  

* Low-grade <u>fever</u>

* <u>Malaise and fatigue</u>

* <u>Myalgia</u>

* Upper respiratory symptoms (e.g., <u>sore throat</u>)

* <u>Pharyngitis</u>, <u>herpangina</u>, and/or <u>rash</u>





> [!TIP]
> Less than half of adult patients have all three features of the <u>classic triad of meningitis</u>; the percentage is even lower in <u>neonates</u> and young <u>infants</u>, who typically present with nonspecific symptoms[[4]](/library/_EY5yI)




> [!TIP]
> <u>Subarachnoid hemorrhage</u> manifests with the <u>classic triad of meningitis</u>, but it typically has a more sudden onset and affected individuals often lose consciousness.




### <u>Physical examination</u> [[31]](/library/S30y3f)[[32]](/library/h30cRf)




* <u>Signs of meningeal irritation</u>

* Neck stiffness

* <u>Kernig sign</u>

* <u>Brudzinski sign</u>

* Systemic signs of inflammation

* <u>Fever</u>

* <u>Hypotension</u>

* <u>Tachycardia</u>

* <u>Signs of increased intracranial pressure</u>:  (< 5% of cases), e.g., <u>cranial nerve palsies</u>, <u>papilledema</u> [[33]](/library/K3aUj4)

* Signs of underlying infections

* Bulging and redness of <u>tympanic membrane</u>: <u>acute otitis media</u>

* <u>Skin</u> manifestations [[34]](/library/jKY_TJ)

* Cutaneous <u>petechiae</u> in <u>meningococcal meningitis</u>: suggestive of meningococcemia

* <u>Maculopapular rash</u> in some viral meningitis types (e.g.,;  <u>West Nile virus</u>, <u>enterovirus</u>)

* Nonblanching <u>rash</u>: raises suspicion for <u>meningococcal meningitis</u> or <u>Rocky Mountain spotted fever</u> (see “Subtypes and variants”)





### Features suggestive of <u>meningoencephalitis</u> [[35]](/library/l5Yv4p)[[36]](/library/A5bR58)




In addition to the features of meningitis, meningoencephalitis is characterized by signs of inflammation of the <u>brain</u> <u>parenchyma</u> (<u>encephalitis</u>).




* <u>Focal neurological signs</u> (e.g., <u>paresis</u>, <u>extrapyramidal symptoms</u>, <u>aphasia</u>)

* <u>Seizures</u> (focal-onset or generalized)

* Behavioral changes, <u>psychosis</u>

* Altered consciousness





![Kernig sign](media/q46j74gz69gwlfmyfayf4g6w.jpg)

Kernig sign

![Brudzinski sign](media/xebptpylztmyp1lssud4dx07.jpg)

Brudzinski sign

## Initial management

### General approach




* Bacterial meningitis is a <u>medical emergency</u> and requires immediate treatment.

* Diagnostic and treatment steps should be initiated simultaneously and empiric treatment should not be delayed for diagnostic steps.

* If the patient is stable and has no <u>LP contraindications</u>: Perform <u>LP</u> as soon as possible before starting <u>empiric antibiotics</u>.

* If the patient is unstable, requires <u>neuroimaging</u> (see <u>criteria for imaging prior to LP in suspected meningitis</u>), or has <u>relative contraindications</u> to <u>LP</u> (e.g., <u>coagulopathy</u>): Defer <u>LP</u> and start <u>empiric antibiotic treatment</u> (see <u>empiric antibiotic therapy for bacterial meningitis</u>). [[5]](/library/hdbcps)





![Management of meningitis](media/pbxpmvksnkic6h9qu2gj4654.jpg)

Management of meningitis




> [!WARNING]
> Do not delay <u>empiric antibiotic therapy</u> in patients suspected of having bacterial meningitis.




### Challenges




* Diagnosis

* There is a significant overlap in presentation between bacterial and other etiologies.

* <u>LP</u> and <u>CSF analysis</u> can be time-consuming and risky.

* Patients may present with relative <u>contraindications to LP</u> (e.g., <u>signs of elevated ICP</u>).

* Treatment

* Bacterial meningitis can be rapidly progressive and life-threatening.

* Patients may present as critically ill and with complications (e.g., <u>sepsis</u>, <u>multiorgan failure</u>) requiring early aggressive <u>supportive care</u>.

* <u>Empiric antibiotic treatment</u> must be initiated as soon as possible (i.e., often prior to diagnosis).

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[5]](/library/hdbcps)[[28]](/library/1db2Ks)[[29]](/library/WdbPKs)[[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)[[38]](/library/zGYrbI)




* Obtain samples immediately for <u>blood cultures</u>, routine laboratory tests, and screening for organ dysfunction.

* Confirm the diagnosis with <u>LP</u> and <u>CSF analysis</u> (if no <u>LP contraindications</u> are present).

* See also “<u>Meningitis in children</u>” and “<u>Neonatal bacterial meningitis</u>.”





> [!TIP]
> Start <u>empiric antibiotics</u> immediately after obtaining <u>blood cultures</u> and <u>CSF</u> samples. If <u>LP</u> is delayed for any reason (e.g., the need for a CT or hemodynamic stabilization), obtain <u>blood cultures</u> and administer <u>antibiotics</u> until it can be performed.




### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[5]](/library/hdbcps)[[28]](/library/1db2Ks)[[29]](/library/WdbPKs)[[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)




* Routine tests

* <u>Blood cultures</u> (two sets): obtain before starting <u>antibiotic</u> therapy

* <u>CBC</u>

* Normal/↑ <u>WBC</u> count

* In severe infections, ↓ <u>WBC</u> count and <u>thrombocytopenia</u>

* <u>BMP</u>: Blood <u>glucose</u> is needed to analyze <u>CSF</u> <u>glucose</u>.

* Common finding: mild <u>electrolyte</u> disturbances (e.g., <u>hyponatremia</u> from <u>SIADH</u>)

* In critically ill patients: possible <u>signs of acute kidney injury</u>

* <u>CRP</u>: elevated  [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)

* Additional tests

* Assess for organ damage and complications.

* <u>Coagulation panel</u>: especially if there is suspicion for <u>disseminated intravascular coagulation</u> (e.g., <u>petechiae</u>, <u>purpura</u>)

* <u>Blood gas</u>: <u>metabolic acidosis</u> may be present in critically ill patients

* Consider testing for atypical infections





### Neuroimaging in meningitis [[24]](/library/iKYJTJ)[[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)[[38]](/library/zGYrbI)




Imaging is not necessary to establish the <u>diagnosis of meningitis</u> in most patients and should only be considered in patients with significant <u>risk factors</u> for complications.




* Indications

* To assess the risk of <u>brain herniation</u> precipitated by <u>LP</u>  [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)

* Identify <u>abscesses</u> or other localized lesions (e.g., in postsurgical patients in whom infection is suspected) [[24]](/library/iKYJTJ)

* Suspected healthcare-associated ventriculitis/meningitis [[24]](/library/iKYJTJ)

* Patients with devices (e.g., <u>CSF</u> shunts) [[24]](/library/iKYJTJ)

* Recommended criteria for imaging prior to LP in suspected meningitis  [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)[[38]](/library/zGYrbI)[[39]](/library/3dbSps)

* <u>Focal neurological deficits</u>

* <u>Altered mental status</u>  [[38]](/library/zGYrbI)

* <u>Immunocompromised</u> status (e.g., <u>HIV</u>, post-transplant, taking <u>immunosuppressants</u>)

* <u>Papilledema</u>

* History of <u>CNS</u> disease (e.g., mass, <u>stroke</u>, <u>abscess</u>)

* <u>Seizures</u> (new-onset)  [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)

* Modalities

* CT head (with or without IV contrast): before <u>LP</u> if <u>increased ICP</u> is suspected  [[40]](/library/Xhb9ct)

* <u>MRI</u> <u>brain</u> with IV contrast and <u>diffusion</u>: especially useful in patients with devices or after <u>surgery</u> [[24]](/library/iKYJTJ)

* Supportive findings

* Usually normal or showing mild meningeal <u>enhancement</u>

* May identify predisposing factors for the infection (e.g., <u>fractures</u>, <u>mastoiditis</u>) or complications (e.g., <u>abscess</u>)

* See “Subtypes and variants” for characteristic findings of specific pathogens.





> [!TIP]
> To remember the indications for imaging before <u>LP</u>, think of <u>LP</u> FAILS: Focal neurological deficits, Altered mental status, Immunocompromised or ↑ ICP, Lesions (space-occupying lesions in the <u>brain</u>), Seizures.




### <u>Cerebrospinal fluid analysis</u>




<u>Lumbar puncture</u> is indicated in all patients with suspected meningitis (see “<u>Lumbar puncture</u>” for details on indications, <u>LP contraindications</u>, procedural steps, and complications).




![Lumbar puncture (1/2): materials, patient positioning, and puncture site](media/j53m62t0u4ehe7rjlyq1p6j0.jpg)

Lumbar puncture (1/2): materials, patient positioning, and puncture site

Lumbar puncture (2/2): procedure

![How to do a lumbar puncture](media/small_6104243c2c2d5.jpg)

How to do a lumbar puncture




#### Interpretation of <u>CSF analysis</u>




* Confirmatory findings: <u>pathogen</u> identification on <u>CSF</u>  OR positive <u>blood cultures</u> in a patient with highly suggestive <u>CSF</u> findings

* Highly suggestive findings: <u>pleocytosis</u> (granulocytic or <u>lymphocytic</u>), low <u>glucose</u>, high protein

* Nonspecific findings: high <u>opening pressure</u>

#### Atypical <u>pathogen</u> testing




Atypical <u>pathogen</u> testing is not necessary for all patients and should be performed as directed by clinical suspicion.

|  | <br><u>Tuberculous meningitis</u> [[42]](/library/HdbKrs)<br> | <br><u>Lyme meningitis</u> [[43]](/library/GdbBrs)<br> | <br><u>Cryptococcal meningitis</u> [[44]](/library/tdbX7s)<br> |
| Appearance | <br>* Clear fluid with a spiderweb clot<br><br> | <br>* Clear fluid<br><br> | <br>* Cloudy fluid<br><br> |
| <br>Cell count and differential<br> | <br><br>* Variable cell count (30–300 /mm³)  [[42]](/library/HdbKrs)<br><br>* <u>Pleocytosis</u> (predominantly <u>lymphocytes</u> but also <u>granulocytes</u> and <u>mononuclear cells</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Variable cell count (10–1000 /mm³)<br><br>* <u>Pleocytosis</u> (<u>lymphocytes</u>, <u>mononuclear cells</u>) [[43]](/library/GdbBrs)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Variable cell count (20–200 /mm³)<br><br>* <u>Pleocytosis</u> (<u>lymphocytes</u>) [[44]](/library/tdbX7s)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Opening pressure</u> | <br>* ↑↑<br><br> | <br>* ↑↑<br><br> | <br>* ↑↑<br><br> |
| <br><u>Lactate</u> [[38]](/library/zGYrbI)<br> | <br>* ↑<br><br> | <br>* Variable<br><br> | <br>* ↑<br><br> |
| Protein | <br>* ↑<br><br> | <br>* Normal or ↑ [[43]](/library/GdbBrs)<br><br> | <br>* ↑ [[44]](/library/tdbX7s)<br><br> |
| <u>Glucose</u> | <br>* ↓<br><br> | <br>* Normal or ↓<br><br> | <br>* ↓ [[44]](/library/tdbX7s)<br><br> |





### Additional microbiological testing




* Special microbiological stains

* <u>Acid-fast staining</u>: if there is suspicion for <u>tuberculous meningitis</u>

* <u>India ink preparation</u>: if there is suspicion for <u>cryptococcus</u>

* Wright or <u>Giemsa stain</u>: if there is suspicion for <u>toxoplasmosis</u>

* Special cultures [[39]](/library/3dbSps)

* Viral culture

* Not typically recommended

* May confirm <u>enterovirus</u>, <u>herpes simplex virus infection</u>

* <u>M. tuberculosis</u> cultures: Results can take up to 6 weeks.  [[39]](/library/3dbSps)

* Fungal cultures: for the identification of <u>Candida</u> spp., <u>Cryptococcus</u> spp.  [[39]](/library/3dbSps)

* For patients with <u>CSF</u> shunts or drains: Extend <u>CSF</u> cultures for at least 10 days.

* <u>PCR</u> for viral meningitis and specific bacterial subtypes  [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)[[38]](/library/zGYrbI)

* Indications

* Confirmation of viral meningitis/<u>encephalitis</u> (e.g., <u>HSV</u>)

* Detection of intracellular bacteria (e.g., <u>TB</u>, <u>rickettsial infections</u>)

* Disadvantages

* No <u>antibiotic sensitivity</u> data for bacterial infections

* Not readily available for unusual pathogens (especially bacteria)

* <u>Latex agglutination test</u> [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)

* Bacterial <u>antigen</u> detection 

* Not routinely used because of variable <u>accuracy</u>  [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)

* Consider in patients in whom there is strong suspicion for bacterial meningitis despite negative <u>Gram stain</u> or culture after 48 hours

* Fungal latex agglutinations: especially relevant for <u>cryptococcal</u> <u>antigen</u> testing (see <u>cryptococcal meningitis</u>)

---

## Treatment

### Approach




* Apply appropriate <u>isolation precautions</u>.

* Stabilize the patient as needed.

* Administer <u>empiric antibiotics</u> as soon as possible, preferably within 1 hour (see <u>empiric antibiotic therapy for bacterial meningitis</u>).

* If <u>LP</u> can be performed rapidly, administer <u>antibiotics</u> and <u>adjuvant therapy</u> (e.g., <u>dexamethasone</u>) after obtaining <u>CSF</u>.

* If <u>LP</u> is delayed (e.g., because <u>neuroimaging</u> is required), administer <u>antibiotics</u> and <u>adjuvant therapy</u> (e.g., <u>dexamethasone</u>) immediately.

* Add other <u>antimicrobial therapy</u> (e.g., antivirals, <u>antifungals</u>) as needed (see “Subtypes and variants” for details).

* Consult the infectious disease team.

* Tailor <u>antimicrobial therapy</u> once the <u>pathogen</u> is identified.

* Provide <u>postexposure prophylaxis</u> for close contacts if indicated (see <u>postexposure chemoprophylaxis for bacterial meningitis</u>).

* See also “<u>Meningitis in children</u>” and “<u>Neonatal meningitis</u>.”





![Management of meningitis](media/pbxpmvksnkic6h9qu2gj4654.jpg)

Management of meningitis




> [!WARNING]
> Do not delay administering <u>antibiotics</u> if <u>neuroimaging</u> is indicated prior to <u>LP</u>. Obtain <u>blood cultures</u>, start <u>antibiotics</u> (and <u>steroids</u>, if needed) immediately, then proceed with the CT and <u>LP</u>.




### Immediate stabilization for meningitis




* <u>Airway management</u>: <u>Secure the airway</u> (e.g., intubate) if <u>GCS</u> < 8, the patient has intractable <u>seizures</u>, or there are signs of <u>cerebral herniation</u> (see <u>intubation of patients with high ICP</u>).

* Provide <u>hemodynamic support</u> with fluids and/or <u>vasopressors</u> (see “<u>Fluid resuscitation</u>” and “<u>Sepsis</u>”).

* Identify and reverse any <u>coagulopathy</u> (see “<u>Anticoagulant reversal</u>”).

* Identify and treat <u>elevated ICP</u> (see “<u>ICP management</u>”).





### Antimicrobial therapy for meningitis




#### <u>Empiric antibiotic therapy</u> [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)




* The choice of initial empiric therapy depends primarily on the <u>prevalence</u> of organisms in certain age groups and individual patient <u>risk factors</u> for resistant organisms.

* Factors to consider:

* Epidemiological factors (e.g., local flora, resistance patterns)

* <u>Bioavailability</u>: Antimicrobial agents should cross the <u>blood-brain</u> barrier and higher doses may be needed.

* Individual patient <u>risk factors</u> and comorbidities





| <br>Empiric antibiotic therapy for bacterial meningitis [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
| Patient characteristics | Recommended regimen |
| Age <18 years | <br>* See “<u>Meningitis in children</u>” and “<u>Neonatal bacterial meningitis</u>.”<br><br> |
| Age 18–50 years | <br><br>* <u>Vancomycin</u> DOSAGE [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)<br><br>* PLUS one of the following third-generation <u>cephalosporins</u>:<br><br>* <u>Ceftriaxone</u> (preferred)DOSAGE [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)<br><br>* <u>Cefotaxime</u>  DOSAGE [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)<br><br><br> |
| Age > 50 years | <br><br>* <u>Vancomycin</u>  DOSAGE [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)<br><br>* PLUS <u>ampicillin</u> DOSAGE [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)<br><br>* PLUS one of the following third-generation <u>cephalosporins</u>:<br><br>* <u>Cefotaxime</u> DOSAGE [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)<br><br>* <u>Ceftriaxone</u> DOSAGE [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Immunocompromised</u>  [[45]](/library/39YSMr)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Vancomycin</u> DOSAGE [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)<br><br>* PLUS <u>ampicillin</u> DOSAGE [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)<br><br>* PLUS one of the following:<br><br>* <u>Cefepime</u> DOSAGE [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)<br><br>* <u>Meropenem</u> DOSAGE [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)<br><br><br> |
| <br>Healthcare-associated infections  [[24]](/library/iKYJTJ)<br> | <br><br>* <u>Vancomycin</u> DOSAGE [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)<br><br>* PLUS one of the following antipseudomonal <u>β-lactams</u>: <br><br>* <u>Ceftazidime</u> DOSAGE [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)<br><br>* <u>Cefepime</u> DOSAGE [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)<br><br>* <u>Meropenem</u> DOSAGE [[24]](/library/iKYJTJ)<br><br><br> |
| <br>Suspected rickettsial (e.g., <u>RMSF</u>) or ehrlichial infection  [[46]](/library/R9YlMr)<br> | <br>* Add <u>doxycycline</u> DOSAGE to the empiric regimen.<br><br> |
| <u>Basilar skull fracture</u> | <br><br>* <u>Vancomycin</u> DOSAGE [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)<br><br>* PLUS one of the following third-generation <u>cephalosporins</u>:<br><br>* <u>Cefotaxime</u> DOSAGE [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)<br><br>* <u>Ceftriaxone</u> DOSAGE [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)<br><br><br> |
| Penetrating <u>head trauma</u> | <br><br>* <u>Vancomycin</u> DOSAGE [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)<br><br>* PLUS one of the following:<br><br>* <u>Cefepime</u> DOSAGE [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)<br><br>* <u>Ceftazidime</u> DOSAGE [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)<br><br>* <u>Meropenem</u> DOSAGE [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> <u>Ampicillin</u> is added if patients are at risk of <u>Listeria</u> spp. infection (e.g., <u>newborns</u>, pregnant women, adults > 50 years of age, or <u>immunocompromised</u> patients) because <u>cephalosporins</u> are ineffective against <u>Listeria</u> spp.




#### Empiric therapy for viral meningitis [[46]](/library/R9YlMr)[[47]](/library/U30b3f)




Most cases of viral meningitis (e.g., caused by <u>enteroviruses</u>) can be treated supportively. Specific <u>antiviral therapy</u> is only warranted if viral <u>encephalitis</u> is also suspected (see <u>HSV encephalitis</u> for further details).




* Indications

* Concern for <u>HSV encephalitis</u>, for example:

* Suggestive clinical features (e.g., <u>focal neurological deficits</u>, <u>altered mental status</u>, <u>seizures</u>, behavioral changes, <u>coma</u>)

* Imaging findings (e.g., <u>temporal lobe</u> <u>enhancement</u>)

* <u>CSF</u>: ↑ <u>RBCs</u> despite a nontraumatic <u>LP</u> (suggestive of hemorrhagic <u>encephalitis</u>)

* Concern for other <u>herpesviruses</u>, e.g., <u>VZV</u>, <u>EBV</u>

* Recommended empiric <u>antiviral agent</u>: <u>acyclovir</u> DOSAGE 
* Continue treatment if either <u>HSV</u> or <u>VZV</u> is detected, otherwise discontinue.





> [!WARNING]
> Treatment with <u>acyclovir</u> should be started in all patients who present with typical clinical signs of viral <u>meningoencephalitis</u> and only discontinued after <u>PCR</u> and <u>antibody</u> tests are negative for <u>HSV</u> and <u>VZV</u>, even if <u>CSF</u> is initially normal.




#### <u>Pathogen</u>-specific therapy




The decision to narrow therapy should be guided by final <u>culture and sensitivity</u> results, as well as local resistance patterns. We list a few examples of antimicrobial agents that may be used against specific pathogens. For dosages in <u>neonates</u>, see “<u>Empiric antibiotics for neonatal sepsis</u>.”

### <u>Corticosteroids</u> [[38]](/library/zGYrbI)[[52]](/library/IdbYrs)




* Indication: : suspected or proven meningitis due to <u>S. pneumoniae</u> or <u>H. influenzae</u>

* Mechanism: reduces the local and systemic inflammation seen in bacterial meningitis and improves outcomes

* Recommended agent: <u>dexamethasone</u> DOSAGE for 2–4 days [[38]](/library/zGYrbI)[[52]](/library/IdbYrs)

* Should be administered before or concomitant to <u>antibiotics</u> for optimal results  [[38]](/library/zGYrbI)

* Discontinue if a <u>pathogen</u> other than <u>S. pneumoniae</u> or <u>H. influenzae</u> is identified.

* Disadvantages: side effects, e.g., <u>hyperglycemia</u>, <u>GI bleeding</u> [[52]](/library/IdbYrs)

* For pediatric use, see “<u>Meningitis in children</u>.”





> [!WARNING]
> Do not delay <u>antibiotics</u> to administer <u>adjuvant therapy</u>. If <u>dexamethasone</u> is not readily available, start <u>antibiotics</u> immediately.




### Supportive therapy




* <u>Electrolyte repletion</u>

* <u>Analgesics</u> as needed (see <u>pain management</u>)

* <u>Antipyretics</u> as needed

* <u>IV fluids</u> as needed

* IV <u>antiemetics</u> as needed 

* <u>Ondansetron</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Metoclopramide</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Prochlorperazine</u> DOSAGE





### Monitoring and disposition




* Most patients with meningitis require admission; select patients may be considered for outpatient therapy with close follow-up. [[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)

* Serial neuro examinations

* Consultations

* Infectious disease

* Consider also <u>ICU</u> , <u>neurology</u>, neurosurgery  as needed.

---

## Subtypes and variants

### <u>Tuberculous meningitis</u>




See “<u>Tuberculous meningoencephalitis</u>” in “<u>Extrapulmonary tuberculosis</u>.”




### Cryptococcal meningitis




* <u>Pathogen</u>: <u>Cryptococcus neoformans</u> (a type of encapsulated <u>yeast</u>)

* <u>Risk factors</u>

* <u>AIDS</u>

* Exposure to pigeon droppings

* Clinical course: : subacute onset with (low) <u>fever</u>, fatigue, and <u>headaches</u>

* Clinical features

* See section on “Clinical features” above

* <u>Meningeal symptoms</u> are often absent

* Diagnostics [[53]](/library/xjbEcF)

* <u>Cryptococcal</u> <u>antigen</u> testing of <u>CSF</u> and serum

* Highly specific and sensitive [[53]](/library/xjbEcF)

* Typically performed via latex agglutination or <u>enzyme immunoassay</u>

* <u>Lumbar puncture</u>

* High <u>opening pressure</u>

* <u>CSF</u> culture (<u>Sabouraud agar</u>)

* <u>CSF</u> <u>gram staining</u>: India Ink (clear halo), <u>mucicarmine</u> (red inner capsule)

* <u>MRI</u>: <u>gelatinous pseudocysts</u> (soap bubble appearance)

* Treatment [[54]](/library/7jd4bJ0)

* Induction: Intravenous <u>amphotericin B</u> DOSAGE PLUS <u>flucytosine</u>DOSAGE for at least 2 weeks

* Consolidation: <u>fluconazole</u> DOSAGE  for at least 8 weeks

* Maintenance: <u>fluconazole</u> DOSAGE for at least 1 year

* Manage <u>raised ICP</u> with <u>therapeutic lumbar puncture</u>.

* Important consideration: Delay initiation of <u>cART</u> for 4–6 weeks after starting <u>antifungal</u> therapy to reduce the risk of <u>immune reconstitution syndrome</u>.










### <u>Tick-borne diseases</u>




* North America

* See “<u>Lyme meningitis</u>.”

* See “<u>Rocky Mountain spotted fever</u>.”

* See “<u>Ehrlichiosis</u>.”

* Eurasia: See “<u>Tick-borne meningoencephalitis</u>.”





### Primary amebic meningoencephalitis [[55]](/library/kWbmls)




* <u>Pathogen</u>: Naegleria fowleri (colloquially referred to as “<u>brain</u>-eating amoeba”), found in warm freshwater (e.g., ponds, hot springs)

* Route of infection: via contaminated water entering the nose (e.g., while swimming) → invades the <u>CNS</u> directly via the <u>olfactory nerve</u> (perforates the <u>cribriform</u> plate)

* Clinical features: causes fulminant <u>meningoencephalitis</u> with rapid onset

* Diagnosis
* <u>CSF analysis</u> 

* Findings similar to those of bacterial meningitis (e.g., neutrophilic <u>pleocytosis</u>, <u>hypoglycorrhachia</u>, increased <u>CSF</u> protein)

* <u>CSF erythrocytosis</u> (due to hemorrhagic <u>necrosis</u>)

* Microscopy shows <u>trophozoites</u>

* Treatment: <u>amphotericin B</u>, <u>miltefosine</u>

* Prognosis: nearly always fatal  [[56]](/library/v5bAN8)

![Life cycle of Naegleria fowleri](media/j5vc2r4nenz1wlikw20wvlwo.jpg)

References:[[57]](/library/N3a-i4)[[58]](/library/m3aVQ4)[[59]](/library/53aiQ4)[[60]](/library/M3aMQ4)[[61]](/library/L3awQ4)[[62]](/library/iWbJOs)




### <u>Aseptic meningitis</u>




* Etiology [[63]](/library/4Qd3wp0)

* Infectious causes are most commonly <u>viruses</u> (e.g., <u>enteroviruses</u>, <u>HSV</u>, <u>VZV</u>) and less commonly bacteria, fungi, or <u>parasites</u>.

* Noninfectious causes include medications (e.g., <u>NSAIDs</u>), autoimmune diseases (e.g., <u>sarcoidosis</u>), and malignancies (e.g., <u>leptomeningeal metastases</u>). [[64]](/library/Fidgtp0)

* Clinical course: less acute onset than bacterial meningitis, without <u>altered mental status</u> [[65]](/library/7id4Gp0)

* Diagnostics: <u>CSF</u> fluid analysis (if there are no <u>contraindications for lumbar puncture</u>)

* Nonpurulent appearance, variable cell count with <u>elevated lymphocytes</u>

* Negative cultures

* See “<u>Diagnostics for meningitis</u>.”

* Treatment

* Most cases can be treated with <u>supportive care</u>.

* In <u>drug-induced meningitis</u>, the causative medication should be stopped.

* <u>Herpes virus infections</u> (e.g., <u>HSV</u>, <u>VZV</u>) require treatment with IV <u>acyclovir</u>.

* Prognosis: Although full recovery is common, there is a risk of long-term complications, depending on age, overall condition, immune status, and the pathogens involved. [[65]](/library/7id4Gp0)[[66]](/library/QQduDp0)

---

## Complications

### Neurologic




* Most common: <u>sensorineural hearing loss</u> (transient or permanent)

* <u>Focal neurological deficits</u>  [[67]](/library/r3afP4)

* <u>Seizures</u>

* Cognitive impairment

* <u>Spasticity</u> or <u>paresis</u>

* <u>Cerebral edema</u> and <u>elevated ICP</u>

* <u>Communicating hydrocephalus</u>

* <u>Cerebrovascular disease</u>

* Rare: <u>brain abscess</u>; , subdural <u>empyema</u>, arteritis (risk of <u>cerebral infarction</u> and <u>cerebral venous sinus thrombosis</u>), ventriculitis, <u>cerebritis</u>





### Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome




* <u>Epidemiology</u>: : predominantly affects small children and <u>asplenic</u> individuals

* Description: acute primary insufficiency of the <u>adrenal gland</u> most commonly caused by <u>adrenal hemorrhage</u>

* Dangerous complication of a number of diseases but most commonly associated with meningococcal meningitis

* Rarer causes include <u>DIC</u>, endotoxic <u>shock</u>, and septicemia due to other pathogens (e.g., <u>S. pneumoniae</u>)

* Pathophysiology: <u>coagulopathy</u> triggered by <u>endotoxins</u>; , which often leads to hemorrhagic <u>necrosis</u> of the <u>adrenal glands</u>

* Clinical features

* <u>Fever</u>

* <u>Myalgia</u>

* Nonblanching, <u>petechial</u> <u>rash</u> (mostly on trunk and legs); in severe cases, even <u>purpura fulminans</u> with extensive <u>necrosis</u> of the <u>skin</u>

* Severe <u>malaise</u>

* <u>Hypotension</u> or even <u>shock</u>

* Findings of <u>disseminated intravascular coagulation</u>

* Findings of acute <u>adrenal gland failure</u>

* <u>Respiratory failure</u>

* Treatment

* Treatment of the underlying cause (see <u>empiric antibiotic therapy for bacterial meningitis</u> and <u>pathogen-specific therapy in meningitis</u>)

* <u>Parenteral fluid therapy</u> and management of <u>disorders of sodium balance</u>

* <u>Coagulopathy</u> treatment

* Prognosis: fatal without treatment and often fatal even with treatment, particularly if associated with <u>meningococcal infection</u> (> 40% <u>mortality rate</u>) [[68]](/library/o7W0550)

We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.

---

## Prevention

### <u>Primary prevention</u> [[72]](/library/a7WQ450)




* Follow recommended <u>ACIP immunization schedules</u>, particularly for:

* <u>Meningococcal vaccine</u>

* <u>Pneumococcal vaccine</u>

* <u>Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine</u>

* Manage conditions that increase the risk of developing severe infections.

* Promptly treat infections that can spread to the <u>CNS</u> (e.g., <u>mastoiditis</u>, <u>sepsis</u>).

* Prevent <u>vertical transmission</u> of infections to <u>neonates</u>





#### Meningococcal vaccine [[9]](/library/Ef18LT0)[[73]](/library/1L129h0)




* There are three types of <u>meningococcal vaccine</u>.

* Meningococcal ACWY vaccines (protein-conjugate)  [[73]](/library/1L129h0)

* Meningococcal B vaccines (protein-based)  [[73]](/library/1L129h0)

* Pentavalent meningococcal vaccine (<u>MenABCWY</u>)  [[74]](/library/1HW2650)

* The <u>meningococcal vaccination</u> schedule varies widely between countries. 

* In the US <u>vaccination</u> is recommended for:

* <u>Adolescents</u>

* Individuals with <u>risk factors for meningococcal disease</u>

* For further information, see “<u>ACIP immunization schedule</u>.”





> [!TIP]
> Individuals for whom both the meningococcal ACWY and <u>meningococcal B vaccine</u> are indicated at the same visit can be offered the <u>pentavalent meningococcal vaccine</u>. [[74]](/library/1HW2650)




### Prevention of onward transmission




* Follow empiric <u>droplet precautions</u> and then adjust based on the identified <u>pathogen</u>.  [[75]](/library/7Wc45Y0)

* Provide <u>postexposure chemoprophylaxis</u> for close contacts.  [[9]](/library/Ef18LT0)

* During community <u>outbreaks</u> of <u>N. meningitidis</u>: Vaccinate against the circulating <u>serotype</u>. [[9]](/library/Ef18LT0)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Meningococcal disease</u> is a nationally <u>notifiable disease</u>; other etiologies of meningitis may also be reportable depending on local state law. [[76]](/library/wrWhj50)




#### <u>Postexposure chemoprophylaxis</u> [[77]](/library/qq1Cz30)




Administer <u>chemoprophylaxis</u> as soon as possible, preferably within 24 hours of symptom onset in the <u>index patient</u>.  [[9]](/library/Ef18LT0)




| <br>Postexposure chemoprophylaxis for bacterial meningitis [[9]](/library/Ef18LT0)[[77]](/library/qq1Cz30)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <u>Pathogen</u> | Indications | <br>Recommended regimens [[9]](/library/Ef18LT0)<br> |
| <br><u>N. meningitidis</u> [[9]](/library/Ef18LT0)[[78]](/library/O3aIi4)[[79]](/library/lRbvMt)<br> | <br>* All close contacts within 7 days of symptom onset, i.e.:<br><br>* Household members<br><br>* Individuals exposed in a childcare setting<br><br>* Individuals directly exposed to respiratory secretions<br><br>* Passengers on long flights<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Rifampin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE  [[9]](/library/Ef18LT0)<br><br>* OR <u>ceftriaxone</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE  [[9]](/library/Ef18LT0)<br><br>* OR <u>ciprofloxacin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE , should be avoided in: [[9]](/library/Ef18LT0)<br><br>* Pregnant patients (<u>ceftriaxone</u> is preferred)<br><br>* Children (unless there are contraindications to other options)  [[80]](/library/SI1yXR0)<br><br>* Patients residing in areas where <u>fluoroquinolone</u>-resistant <u>N. meningitidis</u> has been detected [[9]](/library/Ef18LT0)<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>H. influenzae</u> [[9]](/library/Ef18LT0) [[81]](/library/A3bROt)<br> | <br><br>* Close contacts<br><br>* All household contacts if anyone in the household meets any of the following criteria:<br><br>* < 12 months of age and has not completed the primary course of <u>Hib vaccines</u><br><br>* ≤ 4 years of age and not up-to-date on age-recommended <u>Hib vaccine</u><br><br>* A child of any age who is <u>immunocompromised</u><br><br>* Childcare facility members (all children and possibly caregivers) if:<br><br>* ≥ 2 cases occur within 60 days<br><br>* AND any child is not up to date on age-recommended <u>Hib vaccine</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Rifampin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE for 4 days [[9]](/library/Ef18LT0)<br><br>* Childcare facility <u>outbreaks</u> : Also offer <u>Hib vaccine</u> if not up to date.<br><br><br> |

## Special patient groups

### Meningitis in children [[6]](/library/Od1IJf0)[[7]](/library/pJ1LE30)[[9]](/library/Ef18LT0)




The following applies to children ≥ 29 days of age. For younger children, see “<u>Neonatal bacterial meningitis</u>.”




#### Etiology [[6]](/library/Od1IJf0)[[9]](/library/Ef18LT0)[[82]](/library/OC1IHQ0)




* Bacterial

* <u>S. pneumonia</u>

* <u>N. meningitidis</u>

* See also “<u>Most common causative agents of bacterial meningitis by age group and underlying condition</u>.”

* Viral

* Most common: <u>enterovirus</u>

* <u>Herpes simplex virus</u> (life-threatening; more common in <u>neonates</u> 1–3 weeks old) [[6]](/library/Od1IJf0)[[9]](/library/Ef18LT0)

* Parechovirus [[7]](/library/pJ1LE30)





> [!TIP]
> Rates of bacterial <u>meningitis in infants and children</u> are declining due to a combination of <u>vaccination</u> against <u>Hib</u> and <u>Streptococcus pneumoniae</u>, <u>prenatal GBS screening</u>, and <u>intrapartum prophylactic antibiotics for GBS</u>. [[72]](/library/a7WQ450)




#### Clinical features [[6]](/library/Od1IJf0)[[82]](/library/OC1IHQ0)[[83]](/library/f4Wkil0)




* Children < 2 years old often have nonspecific symptoms without <u>meningismus</u>.

* Poor appetite, <u>vomiting</u>

* Neurological signs

* <u>Altered mental status</u> (most common): <u>lethargy</u>; , irritability, <u>seizures</u>

* <u>Signs of increased intracranial pressure</u>: bulging <u>fontanelle</u> (in <u>infants</u>), <u>cranial nerve palsies</u>

* <u>Hypotonia</u>, high-pitched crying, abnormal breathing patterns [[83]](/library/f4Wkil0)

* Changes in <u>vital signs</u>

* Temperature instability: <u>hyperthermia</u>, <u>hypothermia</u>

* Abnormal breathing patterns: <u>tachypnea</u>, <u>apnea</u>

* <u>Heart rate</u> changes: <u>tachycardia</u>, <u>bradycardia</u>

* For children ≥ 2 years of age, see “<u>Clinical features of meningitis</u>.”





#### Diagnostics for meningitis in children [[82]](/library/OC1IHQ0)




For <u>neonates</u>, see “<u>Diagnostics for neonatal bacterial meningitis</u>.”




* <u>Diagnostics for meningitis</u> do not differ significantly between adults and children.

* In all <u>neonates</u> and in children with signs of complications , consider <u>neuroimaging</u>. [[72]](/library/a7WQ450)

* <u>Cranial</u> <u>ultrasound</u> (<u>neonates</u>)  [[72]](/library/a7WQ450)[[84]](/library/p7WL550)

* CT/<u>MRI</u> <u>brain</u>  [[72]](/library/a7WQ450)

* A <u>multiplex PCR meningitis panel</u>, if available, may help guide management. [[85]](/library/voWAdm0)

* If < 60 days old (especially < 21 days old): Evaluate for <u>red flag features for HSV in infants</u> and, if indicated, obtain <u>infant HSV testing</u>. [[7]](/library/pJ1LE30)





#### Treatment for meningitis in children [[82]](/library/OC1IHQ0)[[86]](/library/ms1VvR0)




For <u>neonates</u>, see “<u>Management of neonatal bacterial meningitis</u>.”




* <u>Initial management of meningitis</u> does not differ between children and adults.

* For unstable patients, initiate <u>immediate stabilization for meningitis</u>.

* Start empiric <u>antimicrobial therapy</u> as appropriate.

* Consult specialists (infectious disease, intensive care, or <u>neurology</u>) as needed.





##### <u>Empiric antibiotic therapy</u>




The following recommendations are for <u>infants</u> and children ≥ 29 days of age. For <u>neonates</u>, see “<u>Empiric antibiotics for neonatal sepsis</u>.”




* Suspected bacterial meningitis: Start <u>empiric antibiotic therapy</u> with <u>vancomycin</u>  DOSAGE PLUS <u>ceftriaxone</u>. DOSAGE [[9]](/library/Ef18LT0)[[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)

* Suspected viral meningitis in otherwise healthy children : Consider using a meningitis scoring system, e.g., the <u>bacterial meningitis score</u>.   [[86]](/library/ms1VvR0)[[87]](/library/N7W-N50)[[88]](/library/BH1zsR0)

* Elevated meningitis score (indicates bacterial meningitis): Initiate <u>empiric antibiotic therapy</u>.

* Low meningitis score, well-appearing, and no <u>risk factors</u>: Consider discharge, with close follow-up. [[86]](/library/ms1VvR0)[[88]](/library/BH1zsR0)





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>ceftriaxone</u> in <u>neonates</u> because of the risk of <u>kernicterus</u>; use <u>cefotaxime</u> or <u>ceftazidime</u> when possible. [[9]](/library/Ef18LT0)




##### <u>Pathogen</u>-specific management




* Initiate additional therapies if certain pathogens are suspected.

* Suspected <u>HSV</u> meningitis (i.e., <u>infants</u> with <u>red flag features for HSV in infants</u>)  : Add <u>acyclovir</u>. DOSAGE  [[7]](/library/pJ1LE30)[[9]](/library/Ef18LT0)

* Suspected <u>H. influenza</u> or <u>S. pneumonia</u>: Consider <u>dexamethasone</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE if it can be given before or within 1 hour of initial <u>antibiotics</u>.  [[6]](/library/Od1IJf0)[[72]](/library/a7WQ450)

* <u>H. influenzae</u>: all children ≥ 29 days of age  [[9]](/library/Ef18LT0)

* <u>S. pneumonia</u>: Consider for children ≥ 6 weeks of age.  [[9]](/library/Ef18LT0)[[49]](/library/AH1RGR0)

* Once the etiology is known, change from empiric to <u>pathogen-specific therapy in meningitis</u>.





![Bacterial Meningitis Score for Children](media/qb7l0y0dxug5xht1mzbberi0.jpg)

Bacterial Meningitis Score for Children




> [!TIP]
> <u>Glucocorticoids</u> are not recommended in <u>neonates</u> with meningitis because of a paucity of high-quality evidence to support benefits. [[9]](/library/Ef18LT0)[[89]](/library/w7WhL50)




#### Monitoring




* Repeat <u>LP</u> in <u>neonates</u> with gram-negative or <u>HSV</u> meningitis.  [[4]](/library/_EY5yI)[[9]](/library/Ef18LT0)[[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)

* Monitor <u>BMP</u> to help adjust <u>IV fluids</u> and antimicrobial dosages, and to assess for the development of <u>SIADH</u>. [[72]](/library/a7WQ450)





#### Ongoing management [[4]](/library/_EY5yI)[[9]](/library/Ef18LT0)[[37]](/library/4KY3gJ)




* Obtain an audiology evaluation prior to discharge from the hospital.  [[4]](/library/_EY5yI)[[72]](/library/a7WQ450)

* In children with residual neurological defects, refer to appropriate services.  [[72]](/library/a7WQ450)

* The primary medical provider should monitor closely for:

* Subsequent <u>hearing loss</u>

* Delays in <u>child development and milestones</u>  [[4]](/library/_EY5yI)
